one_liner: C++ window, input, audio and sprite library; one hobby benchmark draws static sprites 1.29x faster than raylib, slower than SDL2.
what_it_does: SFML is an object-oriented C++ multimedia library with System, Window, Graphics, Audio and Network modules; current development is 3.x (C++17, latest release 3.1.0, master at 3.2.0) and the 2.x series gets no new features. 2D drawing goes through sf::RenderWindow / sf::RenderTexture: you call draw() on sf::Sprite, sf::Text, convex sf::Shape objects, raw sf::Vertex arrays or an sf::VertexBuffer, and SFML issues OpenGL calls. It is not a drop-in for raylib's C function API, and it is not a vector rasterizer: there is no antialiased path, stroke or gradient fill API of the Skia/Cairo/Blend2D kind.
how_it_is_fast: sf::RenderTarget keeps a render-state cache (last texture id, blend mode, stencil mode, view, client-array pointers) and skips redundant OpenGL state calls between draws. Any draw of 4 or fewer vertices, which covers every sf::Sprite (a 4-vertex triangle strip), is pre-transformed on the CPU into a 4-entry vertex cache so the modelview matrix stays identity and no per-sprite matrix load is issued. Each sprite is still one glDrawArrays from client-side vertex arrays on the legacy fixed-function pipeline; there is no automatic batching (issue #3470, a raylib-style batching request, was closed as a duplicate). In megabunny this cheap per-draw path beat raylib's default rlgl path, which emits per-vertex rlVertex2f/rlTexCoord2f calls into a single 8192-quad batch buffer (about 123 flushes per 1M-sprite frame, derived from rlgl.h defaults), but lost to SDL2's batched OpenGL renderer.
when_to_use: You want an object-oriented C++ layer for a window, input, audio, networking and textured 2D sprites under the Zlib licence, on Windows (x86, x64, ARM64), Linux, the BSDs, macOS, iOS or Android.

Games or tools that draw thousands to low hundreds of thousands of sprites per frame one draw() at a time; megabunny measured 12.4M sprite draws per second (roughly 200k per 60 Hz frame, derived) on an unstated machine.
Large sprite counts where you are willing to batch by hand: put all quads sharing a texture into one std::vector<sf::Vertex> or sf::VertexBuffer and issue a single draw call.
Teaching or prototyping in C++ where SFML's tutorials and RAII resource classes matter more than peak draw-call throughput.
when_not_to_use: Vector graphics work (antialiased paths, strokes, gradients, SVG): SFML only draws convex shapes and textured triangles; use Blend2D, ThorVG or another rasterizer from this category.
Maximum sprite throughput without hand batching: SDL2's batched OpenGL renderer was 1.77x faster in the same megabunny table (21.9 vs 12.4 Mbunnies/s, derived from page data).

Projects that need a modern GPU API: rendering uses legacy OpenGL (glVertexPointer, client-side arrays, fixed-function matrices) or OpenGL ES; the issue to move away from legacy OpenGL (#2423) is open and milestoned for SFML 4.0.0, and Vulkan support is limited to creating window surfaces (2.6.0).
Multithreaded rendering: a render target's OpenGL context is active on one thread at a time, and moving a render target between threads crashes per the RenderTarget docs.
Code written against SFML 2.x, like the benchmark itself, needs porting to 3.x (sf::Sprite must be constructed with a texture, sf::VideoMode takes a Vector2u).

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake; optional macOS frameworks)
integration.dependencies: OpenGL or OpenGL ES; Graphics: FreeType, HarfBuzz, SheenBidi, cpp-unicodelib, stb_image/stb_image_write, qoi; Audio: miniaudio, libogg, libvorbis, libflac, dr_mp3; Network: Mbed TLS, libssh2, wepoll (Windows). Bundled or system copies via SFML_USE_SYSTEM_DEPS.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (3.x); master CMakeLists requires CMake 3.28; minimum compiler versions not documented in the files read
integration.platforms: Windows (x86, x64, ARM64), Linux, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, macOS, iOS, Android (cmake/Config.cmake); Cygwin unsupported
integration.thread_safety: Render targets are bound to an OpenGL context that is current on one thread at a time (setActive); moving a render target between threads is documented to crash. No concurrent drawing.

gotchas: No automatic batching: every window.draw(sprite) becomes one glDrawArrays with client-side arrays, so throughput depends on the driver's per-call cost; batching is manual through vertex arrays or sf::VertexBuffer.

Harness flaw in the only benchmark: each megabunny frame alpha-blends about 0.99 billion pixels (1M overlapping 32x32 sprites after edge clipping, derived), so with no GPU stated the number mixes fill rate with API overhead; the raylib baseline runs at default rlgl settings (one 8192-quad buffer) and also draws an FPS counter; each program ran once, timing includes first-frame setup, and the SFML row is labelled 'C' because main.cpp hard-codes the printf string.

The measured program uses the SFML 2.x API (default-constructed sf::Sprite, two-argument sf::VideoMode) and does not compile against 3.x; the 3.x draw path read here is the same per-sprite design (4-vertex cache, one glDrawArrays), but 3.x was not measured.
In 3.x, Drawable::draw takes RenderStates by value, a copy per draw call; issue #3073 asking to change it was closed as not planned.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (Blend2D, ThorVG, tiny-skia, vkvg, AGG and others) are vector path rasterizers; pick SFML only when you need a windowed GPU sprite and game layer with input and audio rather than antialiased path rendering, and reach for Blend2D or ThorVG for path fills.
verified_claims_summary: In electronstudio/megabunny, a third-party hobby benchmark run once per program, an SFML 2.x build (g++ -O3 via pkg-config) drew one million static 32x32 sprites per frame for 100 frames at 12.4M sprites/s against raylib's C DrawTexture at 9.6 (1.29x, derived from page data) and SDL2's OpenGL renderer at 21.9 (SFML 0.57x, derived). No CPU, GPU, driver, compiler or library versions are given.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-06, master at 3.2.0, 3.1.0 latest release, 2.x feature-frozen) and Zlib-licensed, so copyable, but the only speed evidence is a single hobby run of an old 2.x build against an off-category baseline.
